text.p: These are significant stories in the Nigerian press on Thursday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.
- Winners in Saturday's local council elections will be sworn-in on Monday, effectively restoring democracy at grassroots level.
- Queues for gasoline back in Lagos; state oil firm attributes latest shortage to delay in discharging 19,000 metric tonnes of fuel at Atlas Cove jetty in Apapa port, Lagos.
- The export of natural gas by Nigeria, due to begin in October 1999, will earn the nation $1 billion annually, says the Nigeria Liquefied Natural Gas Company Limited.
- Oil companies operating in Nigeria get 60-day ultimatum from the Federal Enviromental Protection Agency to submit comprehensive data on their dump sites.
- Akwa Ibom state in the southeast plans is to cultivate cassava on a large scale for export, says its military administrator Navy Captain Joseph Adeusi.
- Ten more ailing banks have been put up for sale, the head of the Nigerian deposit insurance agency, the regulatory body, John Ebhodaghe, says without disclosing their names.

- Aides of former oil minister Don Etiebet, now leader of the National Centre Party of Nigeria which performed badly in Saturday's local council election, give conflicting reports of his whereabouts. Some say he has been freed after being arrested at the weekend but others say he is still being held.
- Eight persons have been arrested and a warehouse where they produce fake letters to dupe businessmen sealed.
- Four of Nigeria's five political parties begin talks about possibly merger just days after local council elections in which they were beaten by the United Congress Party of Nigeria.
- Oil firms put funds owed them by Nigeria under its cash call joint venture obligations at $1.1 billion.
